hook.text: Wells Fargo employees opened 3.5 million fake accounts without customer consent.

buildup.text: Employees faced extreme pressure to cross-sell products. Each banker had to open 8 accounts per customer per day.

discovery.text: The scandal cost Wells Fargo $3 billion in fines and its CEO.

twist.text: Employees had warned management for years. Internal complaints were ignored because the fraud was profitable.

climax.text: Wells Fargo's scandal showed that toxic sales culture creates systemic fraud.

punchline.text: 3.5 million fake accounts. Years of warnings ignored. Profit beat ethics.

quiz.question: How many fake accounts did Wells Fargo employees create?

hook.text: Enron's fraud couldn't have happened without banks. JPMorgan, Citibank.

buildup.text: Enron needed to hide debt to keep its stock price high.

discovery.text: JPMorgan used shell companies in the Cayman Islands called 'Mahonia' to funnel money as fake commodity trades to Enron.

twist.text: Banks paid $7.2 billion in settlements. They claimed they didn't know about the fraud.

climax.text: Enron was the fraud. Banks were the infrastructure. Without Wall Street's creative accounting.

punchline.text: $7.2 billion in fines. Banks built Enron's fraud infrastructure. They knew.

quiz.question: What role did banks play in Enron's fraud?
options: They designed financial structures to hide Enron's debt

hook.text: Bernie Madoff ran a $65 billion Ponzi scheme for decades.

buildup.text: Madoff's returns were impossibly consistent: 10-12% every year regardless of market conditions.

discovery.text: JPMorgan filed a suspicious activity report with UK authorities but not with US regulators.

twist.text: JPMorgan paid $2.6 billion for failing to report suspicious activity.

climax.text: Banks are supposed to be the first line of defense against fraud.

punchline.text: $65 billion Ponzi. Banks saw red flags. They chose fees over reporting.

quiz.question: Why didn't JPMorgan report Madoff to US authorities?
options: They suspected fraud but profited from the banking relationship

hook.text: Wirecard claimed $2.1 billion in bank accounts that didn't exist. Germany's fintech star was a complete fabrication.

buildup.text: Wirecard was a German payment processor worth $28 billion. It joined the DAX 30 index, replacing Commerzbank.

discovery.text: Journalists at the Financial Times found that Wirecard's Asian revenue was fake.

twist.text: German regulators investigated the journalists, not Wirecard.

climax.text: Wirecard showed that regulators can become protectors of fraud.

punchline.text: $2.1 billion that never existed. Regulators attacked the journalists.

quiz.question: What did German regulators do when Wirecard fraud was alleged?
options: Investigated the journalists and banned short-selling Wirecard stock

topics.title: Savings and Loan Fraud of the 1980s

hook.text: The 1980s S&L crisis cost taxpayers $132 billion. Deregulation let savings banks gamble with depositor money.

buildup.text: Savings and loan banks were designed for home mortgages.

discovery.text: Over 1,000 S&Ls failed. Many were run by fraudsters who used depositor money for luxury lifestyles and bad investments.

twist.text: Charles Keating bribed five US senators to stop regulators from investigating his Lincoln Savings.

climax.text: The S&L crisis proved that deregulation without oversight invites fraud.

punchline.text: $132 billion in losses. 1,000 banks failed.

quiz.question: What caused the savings and loan crisis?
options: Deregulation that let S&Ls make risky investments while deposits stayed insured

hook.text: LIBOR set interest rates for $350 trillion in financial products.

buildup.text: LIBOR was calculated from self-reported borrowing rates from major banks. No one verified the numbers.

discovery.text: Traders at Barclays, UBS, and Deutsche Bank colluded to manipulate LIBOR.

twist.text: During the 2008 crisis, banks reported artificially low LIBOR to appear healthier.

climax.text: LIBOR fraud affected every mortgage, student loan, and credit card on Earth.

punchline.text: $350 trillion affected. Banks rigged the most trusted rate. LIBOR was a lie.

quiz.question: How much in financial products was affected by LIBOR manipulation?

hook.text: Banks rigged the $6.6 trillion-a-day foreign exchange market.

buildup.text: Currency rates are 'fixed' daily at 4 PM London time. Banks used the fixing window to manipulate rates for profit.

discovery.text: Traders coordinated via Bloomberg chat rooms. They shared client orders and timed trades to move the fix in their favor.

twist.text: Six banks paid $5.6 billion in fines. But no senior executives went to prison.

climax.text: Forex rigging showed that traders will collude whenever supervision is weak.

punchline.text: 'The Cartel.' $5.6 billion in fines. The forex market was rigged for years.

quiz.question: What were the chat rooms used by forex-rigging traders called?

hook.text: For decades, five banks met twice daily to 'fix' the gold price.

buildup.text: The London Gold Fix started in 1919. Five banks set the benchmark price used globally for gold trading and contracts.

discovery.text: Deutsche Bank, UBS, and HSBC were found spoofing gold markets.

twist.text: Deutsche Bank turned on its co-conspirators, providing chat logs and evidence to regulators for reduced punishment.

climax.text: Gold price manipulation meant every gold contract, ETF, and mining deal was based on a rigged number.

punchline.text: Five banks fixed gold prices since 1919. They also fixed them for profit.

quiz.question: How did banks manipulate the gold price?
options: Spoofing with fake orders to move prices and then trading against them

hook.text: Banks sold $2 trillion in toxic mortgage securities rated AAA. They knew the mortgages were bad. They sold them anyway.

buildup.text: Banks bundled subprime mortgages into securities and paid rating agencies to stamp them AAA.

discovery.text: Goldman Sachs created a product called Abacus, designed to fail, then bet against it.

twist.text: The fraud collapsed the global economy. 8.7 million jobs lost. $11 trillion in household wealth vanished.

climax.text: Mortgage fraud was the biggest financial scandal in history.

punchline.text: $11 trillion in losses. Banks knew. No one imprisoned. The system failed.

quiz.question: What did Goldman Sachs do with its Abacus product?
options: Sold it to clients while secretly betting it would fail

hook.text: JPMorgan traders placed millions of fake orders they never intended to fill.

buildup.text: Spoofing means placing large buy or sell orders to create the appearance of demand.

discovery.text: JPMorgan's precious metals desk spoofed markets for 8 years.

twist.text: JPMorgan paid $920 million and admitted to criminal conduct. It was the largest spoofing penalty in history.

climax.text: Spoofing is market manipulation using ghosts. Orders that were never real moved prices affecting real people.

punchline.text: $920 million fine. 8 years of fake orders. Ghost trades moved real prices.

quiz.question: What is 'spoofing' in financial markets?
options: Placing fake orders to move prices then canceling before execution

hook.text: HSBC laundered $881 million for Mexican drug cartels. The bank designed deposit boxes sized for cartel cash.

buildup.text: Between 2006 and 2010, HSBC's Mexican branch moved billions in suspicious cash.

discovery.text: HSBC also processed transactions for countries under US sanctions: Iran, Libya, Sudan, and Burma.

twist.text: No HSBC executive went to prison. The bank paid $1.9 billion — about five weeks of profit.

climax.text: HSBC proved that banks can launder cartel money and survive. Too big to fail means too big to jail.

punchline.text: $881 million in cartel cash. Five weeks of profit as a fine. No one jailed.

quiz.question: Why didn't HSBC executives go to prison for money laundering?
options: The bank was deemed too big to prosecute criminally

hook.text: $230 billion in suspicious money flowed through Danske Bank's Estonian branch.

buildup.text: From 2007 to 2015, Danske Bank's tiny Estonian branch processed transactions from Russian oligarchs and shell companies.

discovery.text: A single whistleblower, Howard Wilkinson, reported the suspicious flows. Management dismissed his concerns for years.

twist.text: Danske Bank's CEO resigned, its stock dropped 50%, and Denmark's reputation as a clean financial center was destroyed.

climax.text: A small branch in Estonia laundered more money than Denmark's entire GDP.

punchline.text: $230 billion laundered. One whistleblower. Years of ignored warnings.

quiz.question: How much suspicious money flowed through Danske Bank's Estonian branch?

hook.text: Credit Suisse hid money for dictators, drug dealers, and human traffickers.

buildup.text: Swiss banking secrecy made Switzerland the world's haven for hidden wealth.

discovery.text: The 'Suisse Secrets' leak showed accounts for Egypt's Hosni Mubarak, Venezuelan officials.

twist.text: Credit Suisse collapsed in 2023 and was absorbed by UBS.

climax.text: Credit Suisse's death proved that reputation damage accumulates.

punchline.text: 167 years of history. Dictators' money. Scandals accumulated. Then collapse.

quiz.question: What ultimately happened to Credit Suisse?
options: It collapsed in 2023 after years of accumulated scandals

hook.text: 11.5 million documents leaked from law firm Mossack Fonseca.

buildup.text: Banks created shell companies in Panama, the British Virgin Islands.

discovery.text: The Papers exposed heads of state, celebrities, and criminals using the same offshore structures.

twist.text: Iceland's prime minister resigned within days. But most countries did nothing.

climax.text: The Panama Papers showed that tax evasion is a service that banks sell.

punchline.text: 11.5 million leaked files. One PM resigned. Most offshore money stayed hidden.

quiz.question: What did the Panama Papers reveal?
options: How banks helped the wealthy hide money in offshore shell companies

hook.text: The FinCEN Files showed banks filed 2 million suspicious activity reports but kept processing transactions.

buildup.text: US law requires banks to report suspicious transactions to FinCEN.

discovery.text: Banks treated SARs as paperwork, not action items. Filing the report was the end of their obligation.

twist.text: FinCEN receives 2 million reports annually with only 300 analysts to review them. The system is designed to fail.

climax.text: The FinCEN Files proved the anti-money-laundering system is theater. Banks report. No one investigates.

punchline.text: $2 trillion flagged. 2 million reports. 300 analysts. Compliance theater.

quiz.question: What happens after banks file suspicious activity reports?
options: Very little — FinCEN has only 300 analysts for 2 million annual reports

hook.text: Nick Leeson lost $1.4 billion and destroyed Barings Bank in 1995. One trader sank a 233-year-old institution.

buildup.text: Leeson traded derivatives from Barings' Singapore office. He hid losses in a secret account numbered 88888.

discovery.text: Leeson doubled down on losing bets, hoping the market would recover. Each loss led to a bigger bet.

twist.text: Barings had no risk oversight in Singapore. Leeson was both the trader making bets and the manager reporting results.

climax.text: Leeson didn't start as a criminal. He hid one small loss, then another.

punchline.text: One trader. One hidden account. 233 years of banking history, destroyed.

quiz.question: What was the fundamental oversight failure at Barings?
options: Leeson was both the trader and the one reporting his own results

hook.text: Jérôme Kerviel at Société Générale built a hidden €50 billion position — more than the bank's entire market value.

buildup.text: Kerviel was a junior trader in Paris. He bypassed controls using his knowledge of back office systems from a prior role.

discovery.text: The losses reached €4.9 billion when the bank discovered and unwound his positions.

twist.text: Kerviel claimed his managers knew about his positions.

climax.text: Banks celebrated Kerviel's profits and ignored his methods.

punchline.text: €50 billion in hidden bets. Profitable? Hero. Unprofitable? Rogue trader.

quiz.question: How large was Kerviel's hidden position compared to Société Générale?
options: Larger than the bank's entire market value

hook.text: JPMorgan's 'London Whale' lost $6.2 billion in 2012. The bank's CEO initially dismissed it as 'a tempest in a teapot.'

buildup.text: Bruno Iksil, a trader in London, built massive credit derivative positions meant to hedge the bank's portfolio.

discovery.text: Other hedge funds noticed Iksil's huge positions and traded against him.

twist.text: JPMorgan's risk models had been changed to hide the growing losses.

climax.text: The Whale proved that even JPMorgan — the strongest bank — had hidden risks.

punchline.text: $6.2 billion lost. Risk models altered to hide it. Even JPMorgan wasn't safe.

quiz.question: How did JPMorgan initially handle the London Whale losses?
options: Altered risk models to hide the growing losses

hook.text: Kweku Adoboli lost $2.3 billion at UBS in 2011. He was a junior London trader who created fake hedges to hide losses.

buildup.text: Adoboli traded ETFs on UBS's Delta One desk. He fabricated offsetting trades so his positions appeared hedged.

discovery.text: Adoboli confessed when his losses became unmanageable.

twist.text: UBS had suffered a rogue trading scandal before with Dillon Read. They promised reforms.

climax.text: Repeat scandals prove that banks don't learn from rogue traders.

punchline.text: $2.3 billion lost. Same bank, same failure, different trader. Banks don't learn.

quiz.question: What made UBS's rogue trading scandal especially notable?
options: UBS had already had a rogue trading scandal and promised reforms

hook.text: Every decade produces new rogue traders. Despite billions spent on compliance.

buildup.text: The pattern repeats: a trader hides small losses, doubles down, and the losses compound until discovery.

discovery.text: Banks incentivize risk-taking with huge bonuses tied to profits.

twist.text: Rogue traders are always caught after the losses grow massive.

climax.text: Rogue trading isn't a bug in banking — it's a feature of the incentive structure.

punchline.text: Star performer or rogue trader. The only difference is whether the bet won.

quiz.question: Why do rogue trader incidents keep recurring?
options: Banking incentives reward risk-taking while treating oversight as a cost center

hook.text: Banks gave mortgages to people who couldn't repay them, then sold those mortgages as 'safe' investments.

buildup.text: Subprime lenders offered 'teaser' rates: 1-2% for two years, then jumping to 8-10%.

discovery.text: Countrywide Financial originated $97 billion in subprime loans in one year. Volume meant commissions.

twist.text: Loan officers earned commissions for every loan closed, regardless of repayment.

climax.text: Subprime lending wasn't just risky. It was designed to extract fees from people who couldn't afford the terms.

punchline.text: $97 billion in bad loans. Designed to collect fees, not to be repaid.

quiz.question: Why did banks issue subprime mortgages to people who couldn't repay?
options: Loan officers earned commissions per loan regardless of repayment

hook.text: Payday loans charge 400% annual interest. Borrowers pay $15 per $100 every two weeks.

buildup.text: Payday lenders target low-income neighborhoods. The average borrower makes $30,000 a year and takes 8 loans annually.

discovery.text: 75% of payday loan fees come from borrowers who take 10+ loans per year.

twist.text: Major banks funded payday lenders. Wells Fargo and US Bank invested in companies they'd never lend from directly.

climax.text: Payday lending is legal usury. Banks profit from poverty by funding lenders that charge 400% to the most vulnerable.

punchline.text: 400% interest. 80% repeating. Banks funded the lenders targeting the poor.

quiz.question: What percentage of payday loan fees come from repeat borrowers?

hook.text: US banks earned $15 billion annually from overdraft fees. A $5 coffee could trigger a $35 fee — a 700% effective charge.

buildup.text: Banks reordered transactions from largest to smallest.

discovery.text: 80% of overdraft fees came from 9% of account holders — the poorest customers.

twist.text: Banks marketed overdraft 'protection' as a service, framing a $35 fee on a $5 purchase as helping customers.

climax.text: Overdraft fees are a regressive tax on poverty. The poorest customers subsidize free checking for everyone else.

punchline.text: $15 billion in fees. 9% of customers paid 80%. Poverty was the product.

quiz.question: How did banks maximize overdraft fees?
options: Reordering transactions from largest to smallest to trigger more fees

hook.text: Navient steered 60% of borrowers into forbearance instead of income-driven repayment plans.

buildup.text: Student loan servicers earn fees per account. Processing forbearance takes 2 minutes. Processing IDR takes 30 minutes.

discovery.text: Navient's practices added billions in extra interest to borrowers' balances.

twist.text: Navient settled for $1.85 billion in relief. It denied wrongdoing but agreed to cancel $1.7 billion in student loans.

climax.text: Student loan servicing shows misaligned incentives. When servicers profit from borrower confusion.

punchline.text: 2 minutes for the expensive option. 30 for the helpful one.

quiz.question: Why did Navient steer borrowers into forbearance?
options: Processing took 2 minutes vs 30 for cheaper repayment plans

hook.text: For decades, US banks drew red lines on maps around Black neighborhoods and refused to make loans there.

buildup.text: The practice began in the 1930s with federal housing maps.

discovery.text: Redlining created a wealth gap that persists today. Black homeownership is 44% versus 74% for white Americans.

twist.text: Redlining was banned in 1968, but studies show banks still deny loans to Black applicants at higher rates.

climax.text: Redlining was legal segregation through banking. The scars of deliberate exclusion are still visible today.

punchline.text: Banned in 1968. Effects still measurable today. Banking's racist scars remain.

quiz.question: What lasting effect has redlining had?
options: A persistent homeownership and wealth gap between Black and white Americans

hook.text: Dodd-Frank created 400 new rules for banks after the 2008 crash.

buildup.text: The law created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, required stress tests.

discovery.text: The Volcker Rule banned proprietary trading — banks could no longer bet their own money on risky trades.

twist.text: Banks spent $1.5 billion lobbying against Dodd-Frank. By 2018, many provisions were weakened.

climax.text: Dodd-Frank was the response to the worst crisis since 1929.

punchline.text: 400 new rules after 2008. $1.5 billion in lobbying undid many within a decade.

quiz.question: What happened to many Dodd-Frank provisions?
options: Banks spent $1.5 billion lobbying to weaken them within a decade

hook.text: Bank whistleblowers risked careers, relationships, and safety to expose fraud. One received $104 million.

buildup.text: Bradley Birkenfeld exposed UBS's tax evasion scheme. He went to prison first.

discovery.text: Dodd-Frank created financial rewards for whistleblowers: 10-30% of penalties over $1 million from enforcement.

twist.text: Most whistleblowers still face retaliation. They lose their jobs, get blacklisted from the industry.

climax.text: Whistleblowers are banking's immune system. They detect fraud that regulators miss.

punchline.text: They expose billion-dollar fraud. Some get rewards.

quiz.question: What happened to UBS whistleblower Bradley Birkenfeld?
options: He went to prison first, then received $104 million

topics.title: Too Big to Fail, Too Big to Jail

hook.text: Since 2008, banks paid $321 billion in fines. Zero senior executives at major banks went to prison.

buildup.text: Prosecutors argued that jailing bank executives could destabilize the financial system.

discovery.text: Deferred prosecution agreements let banks avoid trial by paying fines and promising reform.

twist.text: Banks budget fines as operating costs. JPMorgan reserved $8.6 billion for legal fees in 2013 — and still profited.

climax.text: When fines are tax-deductible business expenses, enforcement becomes a tax, not a punishment.

punchline.text: $321 billion in fines. Zero top executives jailed.

quiz.question: How do banks treat regulatory fines?
options: As budgeted operating expenses and tax-deductible costs

hook.text: Banks are regulated by dozens of agencies worldwide. Yet scandals keep happening.

buildup.text: US banks face oversight from the Fed, OCC, FDIC, SEC, CFPB, and state regulators.

discovery.text: Regulators earn $80-150K. Bank compliance lawyers earn $500K+.

twist.text: The revolving door — regulators leaving to work at banks they oversaw — creates conflicts of interest at every level.

climax.text: Regulation fails when regulators are outspent, outtalented, and eventually hired by the banks they regulate.

punchline.text: Dozens of agencies. Outspent and outtalented. Then hired by the banks.

quiz.question: What is the 'revolving door' problem in banking regulation?
options: Regulators leaving to work for the banks they previously oversaw

hook.text: Banks paid $321 billion in fines since 2008 but remain more profitable than ever.

buildup.text: After each scandal, banks promise culture change, hire compliance officers, and run ethics training.

discovery.text: Banking's core incentive — maximize short-term profits — conflicts with ethical behavior whenever ethics reduce revenue.

twist.text: Fintech disruption might force change. If customers can leave for transparent alternatives.

climax.text: Banking won't clean up from regulation alone. Real change requires customers who punish bad banks by leaving.

punchline.text: More fines, more reforms, more scandals.

quiz.question: What might finally force banks to change their behavior?
